Lessons.Title: Divide Decimals by Whole Numbers
ExplanationParagraphs: Original IM2021 G5 U05:L24 shares a DECIMAL LESS THAN ONE among a WHOLE NUMBER of groups; this is conceptually different from previous whole÷decimal count-of-groups. Source uses shaded equal-area fraction grid and unit decomposition.

Warm-up original Estimation Exploration asks the value of0.42÷5 and too-low/about-right/too-high predictions. Exact mathematical quotient is0.084, which is EIGHTY-FOUR thousandths (not0.08 or0.8), but source treats estimate and reasoning as an open step.

Activity1 Whole Number Groups source0.8÷4=0.2,0.6÷3=0.2,0.5÷2=0.25 and0.75÷5=0.15. Explain decomposing tenths to hundredths where needed, and teacher reviews original grid groupings and written evidence.

Activity2 Evaluate Expressions source60÷5=12,6÷5=1.2 and0.6÷5=0.12 encourage multiplying/dividing by ten while maintaining place-value unit. Original0.7÷2=0.35 and0.45÷5=0.09. Source reasoning checks inverse multiplication.

Previous accurate fictional0.72÷3 remains optional Edulytiks extension only. The numerical exact selected Practice covers original ten quotients but not open warm-up estimates and source drawings. Independent Edulytiks Cool-down is teacher scored.

Source and assessment limits: independently authored Edulytiks Cool-down with teacher-reviewed drawing/explanation. Original publisher gated Cool-down, standalone student PDF and original image binaries are not individually certified. Numeric exact choices cover only eligible subskills, not the original open source tasks.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Goal: share a FRACTIONAL decimal dividend into a positive whole number of equal groups, a different operation from whole÷small-decimal. The 2021 source connects shaded hundredths grids, whole-number division facts and verbal explanations before presenting less scaffolded decimal quotients.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Warm-up: shade 0.80 of one square in hundredths and partition the eighty equal pieces into four equal groups. Each receives 20 hundredths, or 0.20. Explain why splitting the selected amount into four groups is not the same as counting how many 0.04-sized pieces fit into a whole.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Activity 1 — exact equal shares: 0.72÷3 has seventy-two hundredths shared among three, yielding24 hundredths each, or0.24. The more delicate case 0.5÷2 requires renaming five tenths as50 hundredths before splitting, giving25 hundredths=0.25. Compare another 0.75÷5=0.15 and explain how 15 hundredths ×5 returns75 hundredths.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Activity 2 — connect whole-number facts: use 72÷3=24 to reason 7.2÷3=2.4 and0.72÷3=0.24; keep divisor three fixed while dividend changes place value. Calculate 0.7÷2=0.35 and0.45÷5=0.09 using hundredths. Learners compare a first-party area strip with multiplication-inverse explanations.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Assessment: exact decimals are appropriate numeric checks; equitable partition drawings, identifying the whole, interpreting the dividend/divisor, and partner revisions from the source require teacher review.

KeyConcepts.Title: Share a decimal dividend
KeyConcepts.Definition: A decimal less than one can be shared into equal groups without changing the original whole.

KeyConcepts.Title: Rename tenths as hundredths
KeyConcepts.Definition: Dividing a small count of tenths may be easier when expressed as hundredths.

KeyConcepts.Title: Scale a known whole quotient
KeyConcepts.Definition: The relationship among72÷3,7.2÷3 and0.72÷3 depends on which fractional unit the dividend counts.

Lessons.Title: Divide Decimals by Decimals
ExplanationParagraphs: Original IM2021 G5 U05:L25 counts tenths or hundredths WITHIN decimal dividends, including those greater than1. Source100-cell grids connect decimal quotient to equivalent whole-number division by consistent units.
Warm-up source Number Talk Same/Different:20÷2=10,2÷0.2=10,50÷2=25 and5÷0.2=25. Teacher compares different dividends/divisors that nevertheless have same quotients.

Activity1 Dividing by a Tenth and a Hundredth original Jada's grid shows ONE whole+60 hundredths, so1.6÷0.1=16 and equivalent160÷10=16. Source another diagram shows1.3÷0.01=130 and pupils explain original alternating shaded column/cell patterns. Do not silently replace with1.8÷0.1 or1.35÷0.01 as publisher numbers.

Activity2 Divide Decimals by Decimals source5÷0.1=50,5÷0.01=500,0.5÷0.1=5,0.5÷0.01=50,0.02÷0.01=2 and1.53÷0.01=153. Multiplication inverse checks and decimal-unit language matter more than unexplained digit sliding.

Prior correct fictional1.8÷0.1 and1.35÷0.01 remain optional Edulytiks examples. Numeric practice checks source quotients; original grid diagrams, classification and explanation remain TEACHER_REVIEW_REQUIRED. Independently authored Cool-down separate.

Source and assessment limits: independently authored Edulytiks Cool-down with teacher-reviewed drawing/explanation. Original publisher gated Cool-down, standalone student PDF and original image binaries are not individually certified. Numeric exact choices cover only eligible subskills, not the original open source tasks.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Goal: interpret how many TENTHS or HUNDREDTHS fit in a decimal dividend, including one with both a whole part and fractional part. The source deliberately uses the SAME hundredths-grid picture to compare1.6÷0.1 with160÷10, making choice of units and original whole central to understanding.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Warm-up: describe one complete hundredths square plus sixty further shaded cells. If the full square represents1, the shaded amount is1.60 and contains16 strips of ten hundredths (each0.1). The same 160 individual cells can instead be interpreted as an integer count and grouped into tens, producing160÷10=16, with the unit interpretation stated clearly.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Activity 1 — related interpretations: calculate1.8÷0.1=18 by counting ten tenths per whole and eight more tenths. Compare the whole-count equivalent 180÷10=18. Calculate1.35÷0.01=135 by counting one hundred hundredths from the whole and35 extra hundredths; the decimal dividend is not rounded to1.4 or treated as one whole only.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Activity 2 — contrast divisors: 0.5÷0.1=5 but0.5÷0.01=50, because a fixed half-whole can be cut into five tenths or fifty hundredths. Likewise0.02÷0.01=2 and1.53÷0.01=153. Explain why the quotient can be a whole number even if the dividend is fractional.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Assessment: source requires precise interpretation of unlabeled grid images, multiple possible unit conventions and grouping statements. A checked 18/135/50 alone cannot certify that a learner identified the correct whole and divisor-sized regions; teacher review of representations and explanations remains essential.

KeyConcepts.Definition: Count how many 0.1-sized pieces fit into the decimal amount.

KeyConcepts.Definition: Count hundredths in the decimal total, including the whole part.

KeyConcepts.Definition: Multiplying both positive divisor and dividend by the same factor preserves quotient.

Lessons.Title: Book Drive (optional)
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: PLAN an original school book-sale fundraiser using purchase costs, marked-up selling prices, estimated quantities, decimal subtraction and multiplication, and a defensible range of possible profits. The source explicitly asks students to make assumptions about attendance and demand, not calculate one official profit amount. This optional activity has multiple valid plans.

Warm-up — pricing tradeoff: two fictional student groups buy a book for$7.25. Group A sells at$10.25, earning$3.00 per book. Group B sells at$11.50, earning$4.25. A higher sale price may bring higher profit PER BOOK but does not prove that more books will sell, because demand is uncertain. Do not claim a real sales forecast.

Activity 1 — compare the scenarios: if A sells36 books, it raises$108 in gross profit above purchase cost. If B sells24 books, it raises$102. If B instead sells24 books, A needs exactly34 sales to raise the same$102 because its profit is$3 per sale. Explain what data would actually be needed to predict which school sells more books.

Activity 2 — design an original fair: choose three categories from a fictional supply sheet: science books cost$8.40 and could sell for$11.40, storybooks cost$5.25 and could sell for$7.75, activity books cost$3.60 and could sell for$5.10. If a hypothetical school sells30,24 and40 of those, profit would be 30×$3=$90, 24×$2.50=$60, 40×$1.50=$60: $210 total. State that the number of copies sold, visitor choices and prices are assumptions, not actual market data. Develop too-low, plausible and too-high scenarios with different participation assumptions and explain the uncertainty.

Assessment: a class-designed book fair must include category choice, transparent costs and selling prices, assumptions about visitors/books purchased, multiple plausible totals and justifications. Teacher reviews financial modeling and ethics; neither the fixed$210 fictional example nor any numeric calculator should auto-mark the authentic planning task complete. No publisher price table or licensed illustrations reused.

KeyConcepts.Title: Profit per book
KeyConcepts.Definition: Gross profit from one sale is selling price minus purchase cost, assuming no other expenses.
KeyConcepts.Example: The true net profit may also require other expenses not given.

KeyConcepts.Title: Total gross profit
KeyConcepts.Definition: Estimated category profit is per-book margin times an assumed number sold.
KeyConcepts.Example: Sum only compatible money values to get a modeled total.

KeyConcepts.Title: Models require demand assumptions
KeyConcepts.Definition: A higher mark-up may increase margin but may decrease quantity sold; no demand relationship is automatically given.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Profit=(price−cost)×quantity; the quantity itself is uncertain.
KeyConcepts.Example: Use low/base/high estimates and justify assumed participation.

WorkedExamples.Title: Compare two prices
WorkedExamples.Question: A school pays$7.25 for a book; compare selling at$10.25 or$11.50.
WorkedExamples.Method: First-party fraction-unit model with numeric inverse check. Student diagrams and modeling assumptions remain teacher-reviewed.
Steps: Subtract purchase cost from each selling price.
Find margins$3 and$4.25.
Discuss why margin alone cannot predict demand.
WorkedExamples.Check: A teacher evaluates the explanation of price/attendance uncertainty.

WorkedExamples.Title: Match profits across groups
WorkedExamples.Question: Group B sells24 books at margin$4.25. How many sales at margin$3 would equal its gross profit?
WorkedExamples.Method: First-party fraction-unit model with numeric inverse check. Student diagrams and modeling assumptions remain teacher-reviewed.
Steps: Divide$102 by$3 per book.
State the count with the assumption all sales have the same unit margin.

WorkedExamples.Title: Plan a three-category example
WorkedExamples.Question: Find total hypothetical profit:30 science books at$3 margin,24 stories at$2.50,40 activities at$1.50.
WorkedExamples.Method: First-party fraction-unit model with numeric inverse check. Student diagrams and modeling assumptions remain teacher-reviewed.
Steps: Multiply each count by its own margin.
Add for total, labeling the sales counts as invented planning assumptions.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Infer higher sale price guarantees higher total fundraiser profit
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The number of buyers can change when the price changes, and it is unknown in the scenario.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Separate unit profit from sales quantity and explicitly state demand assumptions.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Label a fictional planning scenario as a real achieved fundraising result
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The source is an estimation/modeling task, not a record of actual transactions.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Mark estimates as conditional, record assumptions and ask a teacher to review the plan.

SummaryPoints: Book-sale profit models require cost, selling price, quantity and any extra expenses to be defined.
Different reasonable price/attendance assumptions lead to different valid totals.
The source's open modeling work cannot be automatically completed by one numeric answer.
